summary.text: Transposing a matrix flips it over its diagonal, so the row positions and column positions trade places.
Transposing twice brings back the original matrix, and a square matrix has the same determinant as its transpose.
On a computer, software often skips moving the data and just reads the same numbers in a different order.

facts.label: Introduced
facts.value: By the mathematician Arthur Cayley in 1858

facts.label: Double flip
facts.value: Taking the transpose twice returns the original matrix

facts.label: Determinant
facts.value: Same as the determinant of the transposed square matrix

items.prompt: A table of numbers has 2 rows and 3 columns. You flip it over its diagonal so rows and columns trade places. What shape results?

options.label: 2 rows and 3 columns again
3 rows and 2 columns
2 rows and 2 columns
3 rows and 3 columns

items.explain: Transposing switches the row and column indices, so an m × n matrix becomes n × m.

items.prompt: You flip a matrix over its diagonal, then flip the result over its diagonal again. What do you end up with?

options.label: The original matrix, exactly as it began
The matrix turned upside down
The matrix with every entry negated
A matrix with doubled entries

items.explain: Transposition is an involution, meaning it undoes itself when repeated.

items.prompt: A student computes the determinant of a square matrix, then wonders whether flipping the matrix over its diagonal would change that number. What is true?

options.label: The sign of the number always flips
The number becomes its reciprocal
The number stays exactly the same
The number always becomes zero

items.explain: A square matrix and its transpose have equal determinants.

items.prompt: A matrix A has 3 rows and 5 columns. You multiply A by its transpose. How big is the result?

options.label: 5 rows and 5 columns
3 rows and 5 columns
5 rows and 3 columns
3 rows and 3 columns

items.explain: For an m by n matrix, A times its transpose is m × m, so here it is a 3 by 3 square.

items.prompt: A program needs to use the transpose of a huge matrix once. How do linear algebra libraries typically avoid the cost of moving all the data?

options.label: They copy the matrix twice to be safe
They store only half of the entries
They read the same data in a different order
They round the entries to save space

items.explain: Libraries let you mark a matrix as transposed, so the same data is accessed in a different order and nothing has to move.

items.prompt: A matrix is stored so that each row sits together in memory. A program must repeatedly work down its columns. What may speed it up?

options.label: Transposing it in memory so columns sit together
Storing a second copy with identical layout
Transposing it only after every operation
Making the rows longer than the columns

items.explain: With rows contiguous, columns are scattered. Physically transposing makes the columns contiguous, which can improve performance.
